inputs.system:
You are a sharp creative director. You turn a brief into concepts that would make a real person stop scrolling.
Rules:
- Every concept explores a DIFFERENT axis (emotional register, format, hook mechanism, visual style, point of view). Name the axis.
- First, list in "cliches" the 6 images anyone would make first for this brief's category (for coffee: latte art, a pour, beans scattered on wood, a flat lay, a mug in bed...). No concept may be built on one of them.
- Something must be HAPPENING in the frame: an action caught halfway, an interruption, a consequence, or one detail that is wrong in an interesting way. Nicely arranged objects are not a concept. Say what is happening in "moment".
- Specific beats generic: concrete places, objects, gestures. Real-world mess beats styling.
- visualPrompt is a production-ready prompt for an image model. Write it like a photographer's caption of a real moment, not a styling brief: who or what, doing what, where in the frame (state what is cropped and the vantage point; never a centred subject), light source, palette.
- Never use stock-photography vocabulary in visualPrompt: shallow depth of field, bokeh, soft focus, blurred background, golden hour, cozy, moody, cinematic, rustic, flat lay, styled. These words make the image model produce the stock look the critic rejects.
- The idea must read with NO text: never hinge it on a clock time, a screen, a label, a sign or a number. Image models get those wrong and the idea collapses. Show it with bodies, objects and consequences.
- Every concept must work as ONE still frame, because even video is animated from a single keyframe. No montages, cuts, sequences, split screens, panels or before/after layouts.
- Do not invent brand names, logos or packaging text the brief does not give you.
- medium: "video" only when motion is the point of the idea; otherwise "image".
- Keep it tight: visualPrompt under 80 words, every other field one or two sentences.

RUBRIC:
# Rubric

The critic and the judge both read this file on every call. Edit it freely on the day:
this is where the taste lives. Keep it concrete and checkable.

## Attention (what makes someone stop scrolling)

- **First-second hook.** Is there one clear thing the eye lands on immediately?
- **Something is happening.** An action caught halfway, an interruption, a consequence. Nicely arranged objects are not an event.
- **Tension or question.** Does it make the viewer want to know what happens next or why?
- **Specificity.** Real-feeling details beat generic ones. A named place, an odd object, a precise gesture.
- **Legibility at thumbnail size.** Does it still read on a phone at a glance?
- **Brief fit.** Would the person who wrote the brief recognise their message without being told?

## Slop flags (any one blocks shipping; list each one you see)

- Generic "AI look": glossy plastic skin, over-smooth gradients, teal-and-orange by default.
- Stock-photo composition: it could be the top stock-library result for its category. Subject centred or posed for the camera, background blurred to bokeh, props arranged rather than used, nothing happening.
- Cliché imagery for the topic (lightbulbs for ideas, handshakes for partnership, brains for AI).
- Mangled anatomy: hands, teeth, eyes, extra limbs.
- Garbled or misspelled text in the image.
- Visual noise: too many competing elements, no focal point.
- Concept and image disagree: a viewer would not get the idea from the picture. Details that differ from the description don't count.
- Made-up brand names, logos or packaging text that the brief did not give.

## Scoring guide

Score the attention criteria above. Do not lower the score because of slop flags: list them instead.
The harness counts them separately, so the score can still show whether a revision got better.

- **9-10:** you would post this as is and expect it to outperform.
- **7-8:** strong hook and clear brief fit; a viewer would likely stop.
- **5-6:** competent but forgettable.
- **3-4:** weak hook or misses the brief.
- **0-2:** broken.

# Rubric

this is where the taste lives. Keep it concrete and checkable.

## Attention (what makes someone stop scrolling)

- **First-second hook.** Is there one clear thing the eye lands on immediately?
- **Something is happening.** An action caught halfway, an interruption, a consequence. Nicely arranged objects are not an event.
- **Tension or question.** Does it make the viewer want to know what happens next or why?
- **Specificity.** Real-feeling details beat generic ones. A named place, an odd object, a precise gesture.
- **Legibility at thumbnail size.** Does it still read on a phone at a glance?
- **Brief fit.** Would the person who wrote the brief recognise their message without being told?

## Slop flags (any one blocks shipping; list each one you see)

- Generic "AI look": glossy plastic skin, over-smooth gradients, teal-and-orange by default.
- Stock-photo composition: it could be the top stock-library result for its category. Subject centred or posed for the camera, background blurred to bokeh, props arranged rather than used, nothing happening.
- Cliché imagery for the topic (lightbulbs for ideas, handshakes for partnership, brains for AI).
- Mangled anatomy: hands, teeth, eyes, extra limbs.
- Garbled or misspelled text in the image.
- Visual noise: too many competing elements, no focal point.
- Concept and image disagree: a viewer would not get the idea from the picture. Details that differ from the description don't count.
- Made-up brand names, logos or packaging text that the brief did not give.

Score the attention criteria above. Do not lower the score because of slop flags: list them instead.

- **7-8:** strong hook and clear brief fit; a viewer would likely stop.
- **5-6:** competent but forgettable.
- **3-4:** weak hook or misses the brief.
- **0-2:** broken.

decisions.message:
# Teenage Engineering EP-133 K.O. II

URL: https://teenage.engineering/products/ep-133

A portable hardware sampler, sequencer and composer built by Teenage Engineering. It pairs a built-in microphone and speaker with pressure-sensitive pads, punch-in effects and a segmented display in a calculator-sized chassis.

Refused the obvious: finger tapping glowing pads in a dark room; flat lay of the device with cables coiled neatly; close-up of the segmented display showing waveforms; hands twisting knobs under colored studio lights; device on a desk next to vinyl records and plants; slow-motion beauty shot rotating on a turntable

8 concepts across axes: format: foley-source documentary, point of view: covert/concealed, visual style: macro/texture, emotional register: deadpan domestic comedy, context: real-world use, not studio, emotional register: quiet grief/memory, hook mechanism: suspended decision, format: chaotic handheld / sibling dynamic
Concepts round 1: 4 matches

c1 vs c2 -> c1: A has a sharper, riskier hook with an immediate stop-scroll action and payoff that directly proves the mic/sampler's core feature, while B's covert-sampling gag is cute but slower and less visually legible at a glance.

c3 vs c4 -> c3 (order-biased or single pass): Option A turns a core product spec (velocity sensitivity) into a visible, audible, specific moment that only this product could deliver, while Option B's junk-drawer gag is funny but says nothing about what the EP-133 actually does.

c5 vs c6 -> c6: B has a sharper, more original emotional hook that showcases the sampling mic in a memorable unexpected context, while A's near-disaster beat feels like a generic busker-cliché stretch that undersells the device's actual sampling capability.

c7 vs c8 -> c8 (order-biased or single pass): B has a stronger physical hook (a snatch-and-grab mid-tap) that reads instantly at thumbnail size and demonstrates durability/fun/multi-user appeal, while A's hovering-thumb indecision is subtle and risks being illegible without narration.
Concepts round 2: 4 matches
c1 vs c3 -> c1: Option A has a stronger, riskier hook (destruction-as-creation) with a clear narrative arc and satisfying payoff, while B is a solid but more conventional spec-demo concept.

c6 vs c8 -> c6: Option A has a sharper, more original hook that reframes the sampler's mic feature through genuine emotional specificity, while B's sibling chaos is a more generic, expected 'durability' demo that undersells the EP-133's actual sampling/sound-capture identity.

c2 vs c4 -> c2: Option A has a stronger hook (sound with no visible source) that highlights the sampler's portability and covert workflow, making the product the engine of the gag rather than a cameo among clutter.

c5 vs c7 -> c5: Option A has a stronger visual hook with real stakes (near-disaster with the shoelace cord) and demonstrates the device's portability and durability in a specific, legible scene, while Option B's concept relies on subtle internal hesitation that's hard to convey visually and risks looking like a static studio demo.
Concepts round 3: 4 matches

c1 vs c6 -> c1: A has a sharper first-second hook (device dragged on gravel) with a clear cause-effect payoff that demonstrates the mic and pads in action, while B is a lovely but slower, more generic emotional vignette that risks underselling the product's sampling/performance features.

c2 vs c3 -> c3 (order-biased or single pass): B turns an invisible spec (pressure-sensitivity) into a visible, audible, single-shot demo with a tight hook, while A's concealed-sampler gag is cute but harder to read at a glance and less clearly tied to the product's core feature.

c5 vs c8 -> c5: The busker concept has a sharper, more specific hook (toe-stomping a pad, near-miss with a shoelace cord) that demonstrates real-world durability and utility more convincingly than the sibling tug-of-war, which risks implying fragility under rough handling.

c4 vs c7 -> c4 (order-biased or single pass): Option A has a sharper, more visual first-second hook (rummaging junk drawer, accidental rimshot) that lands the calculator-sized joke concretely, while Option B's hesitating-thumb beat is harder to read at a glance and relies on internal state that doesn't translate instantly on screen.
Finalists: c1 "The Microphone Doesn't Care What You Feed It", c6 "The Sound of the Room Before It's Gone", c5 "Street Performer's Backup Band"

concepts.title: The Microphone Doesn't Care What You Feed It
concepts.hook: A sampler recording the sound of its own destruction.
concepts.idea: The built-in mic captures the device being dragged across a gravel driveway, turning physical abuse into raw material.
concepts.moment: The sampler scrapes along gravel pulled by its own cable, stones clattering against the chassis; a hand yanks it back and immediately slaps a pad, replaying the exact scrape-crunch as a looped beat.
concepts.visualPrompt: Low vantage from the gravel itself: the EP-133 dragged sideways across driveway stones by a cable trailing out of frame top-right, dust kicking up, chassis scratched. A sneaker enters frame left, stomps the cable to stop it. Overcast daylight, grey gravel, orange chassis the only saturated color.

concepts.title: Waiting Room Composer
concepts.hook: A bored kid turns a DMV ticket number into a bassline.
concepts.idea: In a mundane waiting room, someone secretly samples ambient drone sounds — the hum of fluorescent lights, a cough, a stapler — building a track no one else notices.
concepts.moment: A hand under a clipboard holds the sampler at hip height, thumb tapping a pad; we hear a stapler-chunk loop softly under the room's hum, then a neighbor glances over, confused by the rhythm with no visible source.
concepts.visualPrompt: Waist-high vantage in a municipal waiting room, rows of blue plastic chairs cropped at the edges. A hand holds the EP-133 low against a thigh, mostly hidden by a manila folder, thumb pressing a pad. Fluorescent ceiling light overhead, pale green walls, out-of-focus strangers in background seated.

concepts.title: The Pad That Remembers Pressure
concepts.hook: One finger press replayed at three different forces changes everything.
concepts.idea: Extreme macro on a single pad shows how varying pressure from a fingertip bends the pitch and volume of a snare hit, demonstrating velocity sensitivity as drama, not spec sheet.
concepts.moment: A fingertip presses lightly, then hard, then lightly again on one pad in extreme close-up; each press produces an audibly different snare — soft tick, sharp crack, soft tick — like a tiny conversation.
concepts.visualPrompt: Extreme macro, single rubber pad filling the frame diagonally, fingertip skin ridges visible pressing down off-center. Top-down hard light casting a crisp fingertip shadow across the pad's texture. Background is pure out-of-frame black chassis edge, bottom-left corner only.

concepts.title: Calculator Drawer
concepts.hook: It was hiding in the junk drawer this whole time.
concepts.idea: The sampler sits among actual old calculators, remotes and dead batteries in a kitchen junk drawer, and someone pulls it out mid-search for scissors, surprised to find it making noise.
concepts.moment: A hand rummages through a junk drawer full of twist-ties, a tape measure, dead batteries; fingers close around the EP-133 by mistake, it's pulled up, a pad gets bumped and a rimshot blurts out before the hand catches itself.
concepts.visualPrompt: Top-down vantage into an open kitchen drawer, cluttered with twist ties, a dead TV remote, loose batteries, a tape measure, the EP-133 wedged diagonally among them. A hand enters from the bottom edge, fingers closing around the sampler's edge, knocking a pad. Single overhead kitchen bulb, warm yellow cast, clutter filling the whole frame.

concepts.title: Street Performer's Backup Band
concepts.hook: No drummer, no laptop — just a box the size of his palm.
concepts.idea: A subway busker sets the sampler on the ground next to his open guitar case, triggering a looped drum pattern live while he plays over it, commuters walking past unaware where the beat is coming from.
concepts.moment: The busker stomps a pad with his sneaker toe since his hands are on the guitar; the loop kicks in, a commuter's foot nearly steps on it, he yanks it back by a shoelace-thin cord just in time.
concepts.visualPrompt: Low ground-level vantage in a subway corridor, tiled floor, the EP-133 sitting beside an open guitar case with a few coins. A sneaker toe taps one pad; another pair of unrelated shoes strides through the frame, nearly clipping it. Overhead fluorescent tube light, cold blue-white tile, case velvet deep red.

concepts.title: The Sound of the Room Before It's Gone
concepts.hook: She's sampling her grandmother's kitchen before the house sells.
concepts.idea: In an empty, mostly-packed house, someone uses the built-in mic to capture the creak of a specific cupboard door one last time before movers take it apart, archiving a sound instead of a photo.
concepts.moment: A woman kneels by an open cupboard, holding the sampler toward the hinge; she swings the door slowly, the creak captured, then taps a pad to loop it once, quietly, before standing to leave the empty room.
concepts.visualPrompt: Kneeling vantage inside a nearly empty kitchen, cardboard boxes stacked at frame edges, cupboard door open mid-swing with visible hinge, the EP-133 held close to it in one hand. Daylight through a bare window with no curtains, pale walls, dust motes visible in the light beam.

concepts.title: Punch-In Mistake That Became the Hook
concepts.hook: The best part of the song was an accident he almost erased.
concepts.idea: A producer's thumb hovers to undo a flubbed punch-in effect, but hesitates, replays it, and realizes the mistake sounds better than the original — visible indecision as the whole story.
concepts.moment: A thumb hovers over a pad, pulls back, hovers again; we hear the glitchy punched-in effect loop twice while his head tilts, unsure, then a small nod as he lets it play a third time instead of undoing it.

Desk lamp light from the left, dim room behind reduced to dark shapes, display glow lighting the thumb from below.

concepts.title: Two Kids, One Box, No Rules
concepts.hook: They're fighting over who gets the next four bars.
concepts.idea: Two siblings on a car ride pass the sampler back and forth, each grabbing it mid-pattern to add their own layer, the device becoming a tug-of-war object rather than a precious gadget.
concepts.moment: A kid in the back seat snatches the sampler from his sister's hands mid-tap, her finger dragging off a pad and smearing a note; he immediately punches in his own hit over hers while she reaches to grab it back.
concepts.visualPrompt: Vantage from the car's middle seatbelt buckle looking up, two kids' torsos cropped at the shoulders, one snatching the EP-133 from the other's hands, a finger dragging off a pad mid-motion. Window light behind them overexposed slightly, seat fabric grey, device orange popping against it, motion blur on the grabbing hand only.

matches.reason: A has a sharper, riskier hook with an immediate stop-scroll action and payoff that directly proves the mic/sampler's core feature, while B's covert-sampling gag is cute but slower and less visually legible at a glance.

Option A turns a core product spec (velocity sensitivity) into a visible, audible, specific moment that only this product could deliver, while Option B's junk-drawer gag is funny but says nothing about what the EP-133 actually does.

B has a sharper, more original emotional hook that showcases the sampling mic in a memorable unexpected context, while A's near-disaster beat feels like a generic busker-cliché stretch that undersells the device's actual sampling capability.

B has a stronger physical hook (a snatch-and-grab mid-tap) that reads instantly at thumbnail size and demonstrates durability/fun/multi-user appeal, while A's hovering-thumb indecision is subtle and risks being illegible without narration.
Option A has a stronger, riskier hook (destruction-as-creation) with a clear narrative arc and satisfying payoff, while B is a solid but more conventional spec-demo concept.

Option A has a sharper, more original hook that reframes the sampler's mic feature through genuine emotional specificity, while B's sibling chaos is a more generic, expected 'durability' demo that undersells the EP-133's actual sampling/sound-capture identity.
Option A has a stronger hook (sound with no visible source) that highlights the sampler's portability and covert workflow, making the product the engine of the gag rather than a cameo among clutter.

Option A has a stronger visual hook with real stakes (near-disaster with the shoelace cord) and demonstrates the device's portability and durability in a specific, legible scene, while Option B's concept relies on subtle internal hesitation that's hard to convey visually and risks looking like a static studio demo.

A has a sharper first-second hook (device dragged on gravel) with a clear cause-effect payoff that demonstrates the mic and pads in action, while B is a lovely but slower, more generic emotional vignette that risks underselling the product's sampling/performance features.

B turns an invisible spec (pressure-sensitivity) into a visible, audible, single-shot demo with a tight hook, while A's concealed-sampler gag is cute but harder to read at a glance and less clearly tied to the product's core feature.

The busker concept has a sharper, more specific hook (toe-stomping a pad, near-miss with a shoelace cord) that demonstrates real-world durability and utility more convincingly than the sibling tug-of-war, which risks implying fragility under rough handling.

Option A has a sharper, more visual first-second hook (rummaging junk drawer, accidental rimshot) that lands the calculator-sized joke concretely, while Option B's hesitating-thumb beat is harder to read at a glance and relies on internal state that doesn't translate instantly on screen.

renders.prompt: Low vantage from the gravel itself: the EP-133 dragged sideways across driveway stones by a cable trailing out of frame top-right, dust kicking up, chassis scratched. A sneaker enters frame left, stomps the cable to stop it. Overcast daylight, grey gravel, orange chassis the only saturated color.

slop.evidence: Image shows an orange RC buggy with large wheels being pulled by rope across gravel; there is no EP-133 sampler, no calculator-sized chassis, no pads, no microphone visible anywhere in frame

strengths: Low gravel-level camera angle creates some grit and texture
Rope-pulling action does suggest dragging/abuse premise generically
fixes: Replace the RC car entirely with the EP-133 device itself — its distinctive calculator-shaped white/black chassis with grid of pads and segmented display
Show the device's body actually contacting and scraping the gravel, not wheels rolling over it
Lose the garage/house background, it reads as a kids'-toy video not a product abuse scene
Keep the dragging rope/cord idea but attach it convincingly to the sampler's corner or strap point
Tighten focus so the device is the unmistakable hero, not obscured by a shoe and rope in extreme foreground

renders.prompt: Kneeling vantage inside a nearly empty kitchen, cardboard boxes stacked at frame edges, cupboard door open mid-swing with visible hinge, the EP-133 held close to it in one hand. Daylight through a bare window with no curtains, pale walls, dust motes visible in the light beam.

slop.evidence: The figure's hands are raised near their own face/ears, with no visible sampler device, pad, or microphone held toward the hinge; it reads as someone covering their ears or adjusting headphones, not capturing a sound.

strengths: Good natural window light and warm/cool contrast creates a melancholic, end-of-an-era mood
Empty room with stacked boxes and bare cabinet clearly signals moving-out/packing context
Kneeling pose by an open door/cupboard is a plausible staging for the described action
fixes: Put a small handheld rectangular device clearly in the figure's hands, aimed at the hinge of the door, so the sampling action is legible
Turn the figure slightly more toward the door/hinge rather than straight-on with hands at head height, to clarify what they're doing
Tighten the crop toward the kneeling figure and door hinge, cutting some of the excess side floor space, so the focal point reads instantly at thumbnail size
Remove or minimize the bystander cabinet on the right so attention doesn't split between it and the main subject

renders.prompt: Low ground-level vantage in a subway corridor, tiled floor, the EP-133 sitting beside an open guitar case with a few coins. A sneaker toe taps one pad; another pair of unrelated shoes strides through the frame, nearly clipping it. Overhead fluorescent tube light, cold blue-white tile, case velvet deep red.

slop.evidence: There is no sampler/EP-133 visible anywhere in frame — just a guitar case, coins, and a man's leg mid-stride. A viewer would read this as a street musician photo, not a hardware sampler demo.

slop.flag: Visual noise: too many competing elements, no focal point
slop.evidence: Foreground sneaker, red velvet case lining, distant figures, subway tiles, and overhead lights all compete; nothing points to the product or the stomp-the-pad action.

strengths: Strong sense of place — subway tile, guitar case, coins sells 'busker' context immediately
Dynamic diagonal composition with the kicking leg gives some motion energy
Lighting and grime on the tile floor feel authentic, not overly polished
fixes: Put the actual EP-133 device on the ground near the case, palm-sized, visibly being stomped by the sneaker toe — this is the entire brief and it's missing
Tighten the crop so the device and the foot making contact are the clear subject, pushing the walking commuter and case to the background
Lose the oversized foreground sneaker-in-case shot that currently reads as the hook; replace that framing with the stomp moment on the sampler itself
If keeping the near-miss idea, show a second commuter's foot entering frame near the device, not just coins, to sell the 'almost kicked' tension

renders.prompt: Tight crop on a kneeling woman turned toward an open cupboard, both hands gripping a small rectangular sampler with visible pads, held inches from the swinging door's hinge, her gaze fixed on it. Cardboard boxes faintly visible behind her, one bare cabinet barely in frame. Daylight through a curtainless window, pale walls, dust motes in the beam.

slop.evidence: The object in her hand is a small woven/textured pouch, not an EP-133 sampler (no pads, no segmented display, no calculator-like chassis visible). She is not holding it toward a hinge or cupboard door mechanism; she's looking down at it like a found keepsake.
Generic moving-day scene with cardboard boxes, open wardrobe, soft window light, woman kneeling in jeans and ponytail — reads as a stock 'moving house' photo, not a specific sound-archiving ritual.
No sampler product visible at all, so the core premise (using the EP-133's mic to capture a disappearing sound) is unreadable from the image.

strengths: Good empty-house / moving-day atmosphere with soft directional light
Kneeling pose and focused gaze suggest quiet introspection, fitting the 'grief/memory' axis
fixes: Replace the pouch with a clearly rectangular, calculator-sized hardware device held near the cupboard hinge, not inspected like an object
Reframe her focus and hand toward the actual cupboard door/hinge she's supposedly sampling, not a separate item
Remove the generic wardrobe-rummaging gesture; show her arm extended toward the hinge in a listening/recording posture to sell the specific action
Tighten crop to emphasize the device-to-hinge relationship as the focal point, since right now the focal point is her hair and jeans, not the moment

renders.changeSummary: Added a clearly visible handheld sampler aimed at the hinge, reoriented the figure toward the door instead of her face, tightened the crop, and minimized the extra cabinet to focus attention.

renders.prompt: Tight shot: a woman kneels in profile beside one open cupboard in an emptied kitchen, boxes just out of frame. Both hands grip a small rectangular sampler pressed flat against the door's hinge, her fingertip hovering over a glowing pad button. The door hangs mid-swing, wood worn pale at the hinge edge. Bare window light falls across her forearm and the cupboard's inside grain.

slop.evidence: Woman posed at an angle with off-shoulder top and styled hair, body positioned like a lifestyle stock photo rather than someone absorbed in a private emotional task; the framing emphasizes her figure over the action

strengths: Packed boxes and stripped kitchen clearly establish the moving/leaving context
The small glowing device held against the cupboard hinge is a legible focal point
Quiet, dim lighting suits the somber/memory tone of the brief
fixes: Reframe to show more of her face or expression, even in profile, so the viewer reads concentration/grief rather than just a pose
Angle the body toward the cupboard rather than side-on to the camera, so it looks like genuine absorbed action, not a fashion shot
Simplify the outfit to something ordinary/at-home rather than a styled off-shoulder top, which reads as posed rather than lived-in
Tighten the shot on the hand, device and hinge to sell the specific act of sampling the creak

renders.changeSummary: Pressed the sampler physically against the hinge (not just aimed near it) and cropped tighter on hands+hinge contact so the capturing action is unambiguous even at thumbnail size.

renders.prompt: Tight shot from behind her shoulder: a woman kneels fully facing an open cupboard in an emptied kitchen, boxes stacked just out of frame. She wears a plain worn t-shirt and sweatpants, hair tied back loosely. Both hands grip a small rectangular sampler pressed against the hinge, her brow furrowed in concentration, eyes fixed on the door. The door hangs mid-swing, wood worn pale at the hinge edge. Bare window light falls across her hands and the cupboard's inside grain.

slop.evidence: The woman is kneeling in a hallway facing a door/window, not a cupboard; the device is held up near her head like a frame or camera rather than near a hinge, and there's no visible cupboard with a hinge being swung
Generic moving-boxes-in-background, shot from directly behind with symmetric doorway framing reads like a real-estate/stock 'moving day' photo rather than a specific captured moment

strengths: Packed boxes and bare floor establish the 'house being emptied' context effectively
Soft window light gives a wistful, quiet mood fitting the emotional register
Kneeling pose suggests intimacy and attention to a small detail
fixes: Reframe so the sampler is clearly held toward a cupboard hinge, not up near her face like a camera
Show the cupboard door itself mid-swing so the action of capturing a creak is legible
Tighten composition to isolate her hands, the device, and the hinge as the focal point, cutting the symmetrical hallway/door framing
Lower the camera to pad/hinge height so the viewer reads 'recording a sound from an object' rather than 'taking a photo'

renders.changeSummary: Reangled her body to face the cupboard (shot from behind/beside her shoulder) so the framing reads as absorbed action rather than a posed figure, and swapped the styled off-shoulder top for plain ordinary clothes while adding a visible furrowed expression to sell concentration/grief.

renders.prompt: Tight shot: a woman kneels in profile beside one open cupboard in an emptied kitchen, boxes just out of frame. Both hands grip a small rectangular sampler pressed flat against the door's hinge, her fingertip hovering over a glowing pad button. The door hangs mid-swing, wood worn pale at the hinge edge. Bare window light falls across her forearm and the cupboard's inside grain.

slop.evidence: The device shown is a plain black slab with a single glowing teal button — it has none of the EP-133's actual identity (segmented display, grid of pressure pads, calculator chassis). A viewer familiar with the product won't recognize it, and a viewer unfamiliar with it has no visual cue that this is a sampler rather than a flashlight or remote.
Her pointing finger bends at an odd angle against the device, and the hand holding the unit has slightly indistinct, waxy finger separation.
Overall lighting and skin rendering have a smoothed, slightly plastic quality typical of AI generation, especially on her face and forearm.

strengths: Quiet, still composition fits the 'quiet grief' emotional register well
Empty cabinet, moving boxes, and bare walls clearly signal a house move in progress
Her focused expression and kneeling posture read as a private, intentional moment rather than a staged product shot
fixes: Redesign the device to visibly reference the EP-133: small squarish body, mini keyboard/pad grid, dot-matrix segmented display instead of a single glowing dot
Reposition her hand so it's clearly aiming the built-in mic at the hinge/creak point rather than pressing a button, to sell the 'capturing sound' action
Fix the pointing finger's angle and show clearer finger separation on the hand gripping the device
Add a visual cue of the specific action from the moment — door mid-swing with motion blur, or her head tilted listening — to make the 'sampling a creak' idea unambiguous

renders.prompt:
Shot 1 (3s): Starting on the still: she holds the squarish sampler toward the hinge, pad grid and dot-matrix display catching faint light. Her other hand slowly pushes the cupboard door, swinging it open in a slow arc with visible motion blur on the wood. Camera holds steady, a slow creep forward toward the hinge. Sound: the door's long low creak, her breath held quiet, distant room tone of an empty house, a floorboard tick as she shifts weight.
Shot 2 (3s): She tilts her head slightly, listening, eyes half-closed, thumb settling on a pad; the display's dot-matrix flickers as the creak is captured. Camera drifts to a close side angle on the display and her listening face in profile, never turning to camera. Sound: the tail of the creak fading, a soft electronic confirmation blip from the sampler, silence of the house pressing in behind it.
Shot 3 (2s): She taps the pad once and the looped creak plays back quietly into the empty room, overlapping faintly with the real door's last settle. She rises slowly, device still in hand, camera pulling back and up to reveal the bare walls and stacked boxes around her. Sound: the looped creak repeating softly once more, her footstep on bare floor, then only room tone as she stands still in the doorway light.

slop.flag: Garbled or misspelled text in the image
slop.evidence: Middle frame screen shows nonsensical mirrored/backwards characters like '688Г9]' and 'ОЗИЗ', 'PYE/O' which are not real EP-133 UI text

Device shown is a flattened slab with a teal radial icon and screen full of garbled digits, not recognizable as the EP-133's segmented display and pad grid; in frame 1 the device looks more like a remote/phone than the calculator-style sampler with pads
Final frame: feet/toes look fused and oddly proportioned, barefoot stance reads anatomically off, and hand holding device in frame 3 is small and loosely rendered

strengths: Clear narrative arc across three frames: kneeling at cupboard, close-up interaction with device, then standing alone in emptied room — the grief/memory beat is readable as a sequence
Lighting and packed-up moving boxes sell the 'house sells' context well
Last frame composition (doorway framing, small figure in big empty room) effectively conveys loss and finality
fixes: Redesign the device to actually resemble the EP-133: visible pad grid, small segmented LCD showing simple waveform/BPM, punch-in buttons — ditch the single teal circular icon which reads as a generic remote
Fix the display text so it shows plausible sampler readout (waveform, 'REC', a short number) instead of garbled mirrored characters

Show the actual hinge/cupboard door mid-creak with motion blur or the woman's hand on the door in the key frame so the 'capturing a specific sound' action is unambiguous, not just her looking at a screen
Tighten continuity: in frame 1 she's kneeling by the cupboard with the device out front; by frame 2 the device design changes shape/color — keep the hardware identical across frames
Add a visible loop-pad tap gesture before she stands, so the 'tap to loop it once' beat from the concept actually appears on screen

renders.changeSummary: Redesigned device to match EP-133 (squarish body, pad grid, dot-matrix display), repositioned her hand to aim the mic at the hinge, and added door-swing motion blur plus a listening head tilt to clarify the sampling action.
